newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovnaft sale could hurt Slovak market.
newsitem.headline: Slovnaft sale could hurt Slovak market.

text.p: The sudden sale of a stake in Slovakia's refiner Slovnaft a.s. has further damaged the already poor image of the country's capital market, analysts said.

The state privatisation agency, the National Property Fund (NPF), announced without notice on Tuesday it had approved the sale of a 15 percent stake in Slovnaft to management-led Slovintegra for 384.61 million crowns ($11.5 million).
The fund did not give any further details on the sell-off and its officials, as well as Slovnaft representatives, were not available for further comment.

Analysts said the sale was yet another example of the murky practices that haunt the local capital market and could prompt investors to pull out. The market has already fallen steadily over the past months.
"The volume (of Slovnaft) sold suggests it was a stake from the basic capital, and in this case the implied price was around 155 crowns per a share," said Bohus Betko of ING Barings.
Slovnaft, the most-capitalised issue and one of few blue chips on the Bratislava Stock Exchange, closed at 818 crowns on Monday, down 32 crowns from Friday.
"This kind of deal will have a damaging effect, not only on the company's share, but also on the entire market," Betko added.
The NPF raised similar concerns in 1995 when it sold a 39 percent stake to Slovintegra at an implied prices of 156 crowns per share.

The deal came on the heels of a dismal issue of global depositary receipts (GDRs) which was bailed out at the last minute by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) at a face value of 1,000 crowns per share. The EBRD has since agreed to sell its 10.5 percent stake to the state.
The NPF still holds roughly 10 percent of Slovnaft, which was partially-privatised in the first mass voucher privatisation scheme completed in 1993.
Brokers said that in addition to hurting transparency, the most recent sale would probably further choke already low market liquidity.
"This may be the last hit for the stock market," said one Bratislava-based stock broker who did not wish to be named.
"Very few foreign investors, who are the strongest players to move shares here, will trade on a market with such a bad image as (this one has) at the moment," he added.
"This has nothing to do with free market principles. They act as if there was no capital market here and, in fact, they are killing the market with such deals," the trader said.
Brokers said the reaction from abroad to the sale was immediate, and that they were already seeing queries from foreign investors who hold Slovnaft shares.

"It seems they will want to get rid of their holdings (in Slovnaft)," Betko said. "Why should they keep them when the privatisation implied such a low price per share. They would logically expect the market to approach that sell-off level." -- Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-521-8402 ($ = 33.35 Slovak Crowns)
